title: Invert Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, mirror it: every node's left and right children are swapped, all the way down. Return the root of the inverted tree.
example: Explanation: Every node's children are swapped, so the tree becomes its mirror image.
intuition: A mirrored tree is just "swap my two children, then mirror each child". That definition is already recursive: if both subtrees are inverted and I swap them, the whole tree is inverted. The base case is an empty tree, which is its own mirror.

There is no slower "naive" version worth writing; every correct solution visits each node once. The two real choices are recursion (DFS) and an explicit queue (BFS). Both swap children at every node; the order of visiting does not matter because each swap is independent.
notes: Say it like this: "Inverting is swap-children-at-every-node, so any traversal works. Recursive DFS is O(n) time and O(h) stack; if the tree can be very deep I'd use an iterative BFS with a queue, still O(n) time and O(width) space."
Edge cases: empty tree; single node; completely skewed tree (deep recursion).
Common mistakes: writing root.left = invertTree(root.right); root.right = invertTree(root.left); — the second line uses the already overwritten left. Save one side in a temp first.
Follow-ups: "Do it without recursion?" — BFS queue or DFS with an explicit stack. "Check if a tree is symmetric?" — compare left subtree with the mirror of the right (LC 101). 6.2
simple: Mirror a binary tree: swap the left and right child of every node.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: The natural first solution: recursive DFS.
steps: If root is null, return null.
Recursively invert the left and right subtrees.
Swap them: root.left = invertedRight, root.right = invertedLeft.
Return root.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; the recursion stack is as deep as the tree height h (O(n) for a skewed tree).
approaches.simple: Recursively mirror the two subtrees, then swap them.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Iterative BFS: same O(n) work, but no recursion, so a very deep (skewed) tree cannot overflow the call stack.
steps: Push the root into a queue.
Pop a node, swap its two children.
Push its non-null children; repeat until the queue is empty.
approaches.why: Each node is enqueued and swapped once; the queue holds at most one level, i.e. the max width w (up to n/2).
approaches.simple: Visit nodes level by level with a queue and swap each node's children.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
pattern: Tree DFS (return value up) / BFS levels
problem: Return the maximum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0.
example: Explanation: The longest root-to-leaf path is 3 -> 20 -> 15 (or 3 -> 20 -> 7), which has 3 nodes.
intuition: This is the "return a value up" template in its purest form. If I know the depth of my left subtree and my right subtree, my depth is 1 + max(left, right). A null node has depth 0. Every other "height" question today (diameter, balanced, max path sum) is this function with an extra line.
Alternatively, depth = number of levels, so a BFS that counts levels also works.
notes: Say it like this: "Depth of a node is one plus the larger depth of its children, null is zero — a post-order DFS, O(n) time and O(h) stack. A BFS counting levels is also O(n) and uses O(width) space instead; which is smaller depends on the tree's shape."
Edge cases: null root returns 0; single node returns 1; skewed tree (h = n).
Common mistakes: returning 1 for null; confusing depth counted in nodes (this problem) with height counted in edges (diameter uses edges).
Follow-ups: "Minimum depth?" (LC 111) — careful: a node with one null child is not a leaf, so you can't just take min; BFS stopping at the first leaf is cleanest. 6.3
simple: How many levels does the tree have?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: BFS, counting levels (the most literal reading: "how many levels are there?").
steps: Push the root into a queue; depth = 0.
While the queue is not empty: record size = queue.size(), pop exactly size nodes (one whole level), pushing their children.
After each level, depth++.
approaches.why: Every node is enqueued once; the queue holds at most one full level (width w, up to n/2).
approaches.simple: Walk the tree level by level with a queue and count the levels.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Recursive DFS: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), depth(null) = 0.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; stack depth equals tree height (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed).
approaches.simple: Depth of a node = 1 + the deeper of its two children. Empty tree has depth 0.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
pattern: Tree DFS (return height, update global answer)
problem: The diameter of a binary tree is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root. Return the diameter.
example: Explanation: The longest path is 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 (or 5 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3), which has 3 edges.
intuition: Any path in a tree has one highest node, the "turning point". At that node, the path goes down the left side as far as possible and down the right side as far as possible. So the longest path that turns at node has length height(left) + height(right) edges, where height is measured in nodes (a null child contributes 0).

The answer is the max of that value over all nodes. The brute force recomputes heights for every node. The key optimization: the height function already visits every node and already knows both child heights, so update the global diameter right there, while returning the height upward. One pass.
Trace on [1,2,3,4,5]: height(4)=1, height(5)=1, at node 2: 1+1=2, height(2)=2. height(3)=1. At node 1: 2+1=3 → answer 3.
notes: Say it like this: "Every path has a highest node where it turns, and its length there is leftHeight + rightHeight. Brute force recomputes heights at each node for O(n²). Instead I compute heights bottom-up once and update a global max at every node, which is O(n) time and O(h) stack."
Edge cases: single node → 0 (edges, not nodes); path not through root (e.g., a huge left subtree and tiny right side); skewed tree.
Common mistakes: returning l + r instead of 1 + max(l, r) to the parent (a parent can only extend ONE branch); counting nodes instead of edges; only checking the root.
Follow-ups: "Diameter of an N-ary tree / general tree?" — keep the top two child heights at each node. "Return the actual path?" — also return the deepest node per subtree. 6.4
simple: Find the longest path between any two nodes (counted in edges).

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Write height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), null = 0.
For every node (any traversal), compute height(node.left) + height(node.right).
Return the maximum over all nodes.
approaches.why: height costs O(size of subtree) and is called at every node; for a skewed tree that sums to n + (n−1) +... = O(n²).
approaches.simple: For every node, compute the heights of its two sides from scratch and add them.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: One DFS that returns height and updates a global best.
steps: dfs(null) = 0.
l = dfs(left), r = dfs(right).
best = max(best, l + r) — the path turning at this node.
Return 1 + max(l, r) — the height for the parent.
approaches.why: Each node is processed once with O(1) work; only the recursion stack is extra.
approaches.simple: One trip down the tree: each node returns its height and, on the way, updates the best left-height + right-height.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
problem: A binary tree is height-balanced if, for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Return whether the given tree is balanced.
example: Explanation: At the root, left height = 1 and right height = 2 (diff 1); every other node also differs by at
intuition: The definition says "every node", so the brute force checks each node by computing both heights from scratch: O(n²) on a skewed tree.

Better: compute heights bottom-up once, as in diameter. While returning heights, if any subtree is unbalanced, there's no point continuing — return a sentinel -1 meaning "unbalanced", and let it propagate all the way up. So the function returns either the real height (≥ 0) or −1.
notes: Say it like this: "The brute force checks height difference at every node by recomputing heights, O(n²) worst case. I fold the check into the height computation: return −1 as soon as a subtree is unbalanced, otherwise the height. Single pass, O(n) time, O(h) stack."
Edge cases: empty tree is balanced; a tree balanced at the root but not deeper (e.g., both root children are long chains) — must be false.
Common mistakes: only comparing the root's left and right heights; forgetting to propagate −1 (computing 1 + max(-1, x) turns the sentinel into a valid-looking height).

Follow-ups: "Return the pair (balanced, height) instead of a sentinel?" — fine in Java with a small array/object, the sentinel is just a compact encoding. "Make a BST balanced?" (LC 1382) — inorder to a sorted list, then build from the middle. 6.5
simple: Is the tree balanced (the two sides of every node differ in height by at most 1)?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: If root is null, it is balanced.
Compute height(left) and height(right); if they differ by more than 1, return false.
Recursively require both children to be balanced.
approaches.why: At each node we pay O(subtree size) for heights; on a skewed tree that's O(n²) total. (On a balanced tree it's O(n log n).)
approaches.simple: For every node, compute both heights and compare, then check the children too.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: check(null) = 0.
l = check(left); if −1 return −1. r = check(right); if −1 return −1.
If |l − r| > 1 return −1.
Otherwise return 1 + max(l, r). Tree is balanced iff check(root)!= -1.
approaches.why: Each node is visited at most once (and we stop early on the first imbalance); stack depth is the height.
approaches.simple: Compute heights bottom-up and return −1 as soon as any node is unbalanced, so the answer bubbles up in one pass.

title: Same Tree
pattern: Tree DFS on two trees in parallel
problem: Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, return true if they are structurally identical and every corresponding node has the same value.
example: Explanation: Same shape, same values at every position.
intuition: Two trees are the same if their roots match and their left subtrees are the same and their right subtrees are the same. Walk both trees together. The base cases carry all the logic: both null → same; exactly one null → different; values differ → different.

A brute-force-ish alternative is to turn each tree into a string (including null markers, otherwise different shapes can produce the same traversal) and compare strings. That works but needs O(n) extra memory and can't stop early.
notes: Say it like this: "I could serialize both trees with null markers and compare strings in O(n) time and space. Better is to recurse on both trees together: both null is true, one null or different values is false, else recurse left and right. O(n) time worst case, O(h) stack, and it stops at the first mismatch."
Edge cases: both empty; one empty; same values but different shape ([1,2] vs [1,null,2]).
Common mistakes: serializing without null markers (different shapes collide); checking p.val!= q.val before the null checks (NullPointerException).
Follow-ups: "Symmetric tree?" — same function but compare a.left with b.right. This helper is reused directly in the next problem, Subtree of Another Tree. 6.6
simple: Are two trees exactly the same shape with the same values?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Serialize each tree with a preorder traversal, writing # for null children and a separator between values.
Compare the two strings.
approaches.why: We visit every node of both trees and store both strings, even if the roots differ.
approaches.simple: Write each tree out as text (including empty spots) and compare the texts.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Parallel recursion.
steps: Both null → true. One null → false.
Values differ → false.
Return same(p.left, q.left) && same(p.right, q.right).
approaches.why: We stop at the first mismatch, so at most the smaller tree is walked; stack depth is bounded by the shorter height.
approaches.simple: Compare the roots, then compare left with left and right with right recursively.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
pattern: Tree DFS + Same Tree / Serialization + string matching
problem: Given two binary trees root and subRoot, return true if some node of root has a subtree that is identical (same structure and values) to subRoot. A node's subtree means that node and all its descendants.
example: Explanation: The subtree rooted at root's left child (4 with children 1 and 2) is identical to subRoot.
intuition: "Is subRoot a subtree of root?" means "is there some node in root where isSameTree(node, subRoot) is true?". So walk every node of root and call Same Tree from 6.5. That's O(m·n) in the worst case, and it's what most interviewers expect for this Easy.

To do better, turn the problem into string matching. Serialize both trees in preorder with null markers and a delimiter before every value. A subtree's serialization is a contiguous block in the parent's preorder serialization, and with null markers the reverse holds too. Then use KMP to find S(subRoot) inside S(root) in linear time. The leading delimiter matters: without it, 2,#,# would wrongly match inside 12,#,#.
notes: Say it like this: "At every node of root I check isSameTree with subRoot: O(m·n) time, O(h) space, which is fine for the constraints. For linear time I serialize both trees in preorder with null markers and delimiters, then use KMP to check if one string contains the other: O(m + n) time and space."

Edge cases: subRoot equal to the whole root; values that are prefixes of each other (12 vs 2); negative values (the - is just another character, still fine); root matches subRoot's top but has extra descendants (must be false — that's why null markers matter).
Common mistakes: serializing without null markers; no delimiter before values; using String.contains and claiming O(m + n) (Java's contains is naive O(m·n) worst case).
Follow-ups: "Alternative linear method?" — Merkle hashing: hash each subtree from its children's hashes and compare with subRoot's hash (verify on collision). Lowest Common Ancestor 6.7
simple: Does a smaller tree appear exactly inside a bigger tree?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: If root is null, return false (subRoot is non-null by constraints).
If isSame(root, subRoot), return true.
Otherwise return isSubtree(root.left, subRoot) || isSubtree(root.right, subRoot).
approaches.why: For each of the m nodes of root we may run a comparison costing up to O(n) (size of subRoot); stack depth is the height of root.
approaches.simple: At every node of the big tree, check if the tree starting there is the same as the small tree.

e.t: a === null || b === null || a.val !== b.val
a === null || b === null || a.val !== b.val
a === null || b === null || a.val !== b.val
a === null || b === null || a.val !== b.val

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Serialization + KMP.
steps: Serialize each tree in preorder: each node as,val, each null as,#.
Build the KMP failure (LPS) array for the pattern S(subRoot).
Scan S(root) with KMP; return true if the full pattern is matched.
approaches.why: Serialization is linear in the number of nodes, and KMP is linear in text + pattern length; both strings and the LPS array are stored.
approaches.simple: Write both trees as text and use string matching (KMP) to search the small text inside the big one.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
problem: Given a binary search tree and two nodes p and q that exist in it, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q as descendants (a node counts as a descendant of itself). All values are unique.
example: Explanation: 2 is in the left subtree of 6 and 8 is in the right, so 6 is where their paths split.
intuition: Think of walking down from the root toward both p and q at the same time. As long as both are smaller than the current node, both live in the left subtree, so the LCA is there too. Both larger → go right. The first node where they split (one ≤ node ≤ other) is the LCA: it's an ancestor of both, and any step down would lose one of them. That split also covers the case where the current node equals p or q.
The BST ordering means we never explore both sides — we follow one path of length h, and we don't even need recursion.
notes: Say it like this: "The general binary-tree LCA visits everything, O(n). In a BST, if both values are smaller I go left, both larger I go right, and the first node where they split is the answer. That's O(h) time and O(1) space iteratively."
Edge cases: p is an ancestor of q (answer is p); p == q; skewed BST (h = n).
Common mistakes: using <= in the go-left condition (skips past the answer when the node equals p or q); recursing both sides in a BST (wastes the property).

Follow-ups: "Plain binary tree?" — the brute force above (LC 236). "Nodes might not exist?" — track whether both were actually found. "Parent pointers available?" — it becomes intersection of two linked lists. 6.8
simple: In a binary search tree, find the lowest node that has both p and q below it (or is one of them).

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Ignore the BST property and use the general binary-tree LCA (LC 236).
steps: If node is null, or is p or q, return it.
Recurse left and right.
If both sides returned non-null, p and q are on different sides → this node is the LCA. Otherwise return whichever side is non-null.
approaches.why: It may visit every node because it doesn't use ordering to prune; stack depth is the height.
approaches.simple: Use the general method: search both sides; the node where p and q split is the answer.

e.t: root === null || root === p || root === q
root === null || root === p || root === q
root === null || root === p || root === q

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Iterative BST walk. 1. Start at root. 2. If both p.val and q.val < node.val, go left; if both > node.val, go right.
steps: Otherwise they split here (or one equals this node): return node.
approaches.why: We follow a single root-to-node path, and the loop uses no stack. h is O(log n) for a balanced BST, O(n) for a skewed one.
approaches.simple: Use BST order: if both are smaller go left, if both are bigger go right, otherwise you found the split point.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problem: Return the values of a binary tree level by level, from left to right: a list of lists where the i-th list contains the values at depth i.
example: Explanation: Level 0 has 3, level 1 has 9 and 20, level 2 has 15 and 7.
intuition: A queue naturally outputs nodes in level order: the root, then its children, then their children... The only trick is knowing where one level ends and the next begins. Snapshot size = queue.size() at the start of a level: exactly those size nodes belong to the current level; any children pushed while processing them belong to the next. This "size snapshot" loop is the template for every level-based question.
A naive way is to first compute the height H, then for each level d do a fresh DFS that collects nodes at depth d — correct but repeats work.
notes: Say it like this: "A naive approach does one depth-limited DFS per level, O(n·h). With a BFS queue, I snapshot the queue size at the start of each level so I know exactly which nodes belong to it. Every node is processed once: O(n) time, O(width) extra space."
Edge cases: empty tree → []; single node; skewed tree (each level has one node).
Common mistakes: using queue.size() directly in the for-condition (it changes as you push children); in JS, using shift() on a big array (O(n) each) — use a next-level array or a head index.

Follow-ups: "Zigzag order?" (LC 103) — reverse every other level or add to front. "Bottom-up?" — reverse the result. "DFS version?" — pass depth, result.get(depth).add(val), creating the list when depth == result.size(); O(n) time, O(h) stack. 6.9
simple: List the tree's values level by level.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Compute the tree height H.
For each level d from 0 to H−1, run a DFS from the root that adds node.val when the current depth equals d (left before right, so order is preserved).
Collect each level's list.
approaches.why: Each of the h levels triggers a DFS that can touch up to O(n) nodes (we stop descending at depth d, but in the worst case that's still most of the tree). Extra space is the recursion stack, excluding the output.
approaches.simple: For each depth, walk the whole tree and collect nodes at that depth.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: BFS with a queue and a size snapshot.
steps: Push root (if non-null).
While the queue is non-empty: size = queue.size(); pop size nodes into a new list, pushing their children.
Append the list to the result.
approaches.why: Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once; the queue holds at most one level (max width w, up to n/2), excluding the output.
approaches.simple: Use a queue. Each round, take exactly the nodes of one level and add their children for the next round.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View / Left View
pattern: BFS by level / DFS with depth
problem: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree: return the values of the nodes you can see, top to bottom — that is, the last node of each level. The left view (Striver) is the same with the first node of each level.
example: Explanation: Levels are [1], [2,3], [5,4]; the last of each is 1,3,4 and the first of each is 1,2,5.
intuition: "Right view" sounds like "follow right children", but that's wrong: in [1,2,3,4] node 4 hangs off the left side yet is visible from the right because nothing is to its right on that level. The correct definition is per level: the rightmost node of each depth. So level-order BFS answers it directly.

The slicker DFS version: visit root → right → left and track depth. The first time you reach a new depth (depth == result.size()), that node is the rightmost of that level, because you always try the right side first. For the left view, visit root → left → right.
notes: Say it like this: "The right view is the last node of each level, so a level-order BFS gives it in O(n) time and O(width) space. Alternatively a DFS visiting right before left adds a node whenever it reaches a new depth for the first time — O(n) time, O(h) space. Left view is the same with left visited first."
Edge cases: empty tree; a deeper left subtree poking out below a short right subtree ([1,2,3,4] → [1,3,4]); skewed tree.
Common mistakes: only walking right children; in DFS, checking depth > result.size() or adding every node at a depth (overwriting gives the wrong side if you go left first).
Follow-ups: "Top view / bottom view?" — BFS with horizontal distance (root 0, left −1, right +1) and a TreeMap; first seen per distance is top view, last seen is bottom view. 6.10
simple: What do you see looking at the tree from the right side (or left side)?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Level-order BFS, then pick the last (right view) or first (left view) node of each level. 1. Standard size-snapshot BFS.
steps: In each level, record the node at index size − 1 (right) or index 0 (left).
approaches.why: Every node is processed once; the queue holds one level at a time.
approaches.simple: Go level by level and take the last node of each level (first for the left view).

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: DFS with depth; right child first for the right view, left child first for the left view.
steps: dfs(node, depth): if null, return.
If depth == result.size(), this is the first node seen at this depth → add it.
Recurse into the preferred side first, then the other, with depth + 1.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; only the recursion stack (tree height) is used, which beats O(width) on bushy, shallow trees.
approaches.simple: Depth-first, visiting the right child first. The first node you reach at each new depth is visible.

title: Count Good Nodes In Binary Tree
problem: A node X is "good" if, on the path from the root to X, no node has a value greater than X. Return the number of good nodes. The root is always good.
example: Explanation: Good nodes are 3 (root), 4 (path 3->4), 5 (path 3->4->5), and the 3 in the left subtree (path
intuition: So far we've passed information up (heights). Here the condition depends on the path above the node, so we pass information down. Whether X is good only depends on one number: the maximum value on the path from the root to X's parent. If X.val >= maxSoFar, X is good; then call the children with max(maxSoFar, X.val).
The brute force keeps the whole path and scans it at every node — it works but repeats the same max computation.
notes: Say it like this: "A node is good if it's at least the max of its ancestors. Keeping the whole path and scanning it is O(n·h). Instead I pass the running max down the recursion, so each node is checked in O(1): O(n) time, O(h) space."
Edge cases: single node → 1; equal values (>=, equal counts as good); negative values (start with MIN_VALUE, not 0).
Common mistakes: using > instead of >=; initializing max to 0 (breaks with negative values); updating a shared global max instead of passing it per path (siblings would see each other's values).
Follow-ups: "Iterative?" — stack or queue of (node, maxSoFar) pairs. This "pass state down" pattern also solves Path Sum (LC 112/113) and Sum Root to Leaf Numbers (LC 129). 6.11
simple: A node is good if nothing on the path from the root to it is bigger. Count good nodes.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: DFS while maintaining the current root-to-node path in a list.
At each node, scan the path to see if any value is greater than the node's value.
Count the node if none is; recurse; remove the node from the path when backtracking.
approaches.why: Each node scans a path of length up to h (O(n²) for a skewed tree); the path list and stack are O(h).
approaches.simple: Keep the whole path and scan it at every node.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Pass the running maximum down.
steps: dfs(node, maxSoFar): if null, return
good = node.val >= maxSoFar? 1: 0.
newMax = max(maxSoFar, node.val); return good + dfs(left, newMax) + dfs(right, newMax).
Start with dfs(root, root.val) (or Integer.MIN_VALUE).
approaches.why: O(1) work per node; only the recursion stack.
approaches.simple: Carry only the biggest value seen so far down the tree.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problem: Return true if a binary tree is a valid BST: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller and all values in its right subtree are strictly larger, and both subtrees are BSTs themselves.
example: Explanation: The root is 5 but its right child is 4, which is smaller than 5.
intuition: The classic trap: checking only left.val < node.val < right.val for each node. That misses cases like [5,4,6,null,null,3,7] where 3 is a valid child of 6 but sits in 5's right subtree while being smaller than 5. The rule is about whole subtrees.

Two clean ways to enforce that: - Bounds passed down: every node must lie in an open interval (low, high). Going left, the current value becomes the new upper bound; going right, it becomes the new lower bound. Root starts with (-∞, +∞). - Inorder is sorted: a tree is a BST if and only if its inorder traversal is strictly increasing.
notes: Say it like this: "Checking only parent-child pairs is wrong because the rule covers whole subtrees. The literal check (max of left, min of right at every node) is O(n²). Inorder must be strictly increasing, which gives O(n) with an O(n) list. Best is passing an allowed (low, high) range down: O(n) time, O(h) space."
Edge cases: duplicates ([2,2,2] is invalid — strict inequality); node values equal to Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE (why we use long or null bounds); single node.
Common mistakes: comparing only with direct children; using int sentinels like Integer.MAX_VALUE as bounds; using <= where < is needed.

Follow-ups: "O(1) extra list?" — inorder with a prev variable (still O(h) stack), or Morris traversal for true O(1). "Recover a BST where two nodes were swapped?" (LC 99) — find the two inversions during inorder. 6.12
simple: Is the tree a valid binary search tree?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Check the definition literally at every node.
steps: For each node, compute max(left subtree) and min(right subtree).
Require max(left) < node.val < min(right).
Recurse into both children.
approaches.why: Finding the max/min of a subtree costs O(subtree size) and we do it at every node; for a skewed tree that's quadratic.
approaches.simple: For each node, check that everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is bigger.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: Inorder traversal into a list, then check that it's strictly increasing.
steps: Inorder (left, node, right) collects values.
For every i, require list[i-1] < list[i].
approaches.why: One traversal plus one scan, but we store all n values.
approaches.simple: An in-order walk of a valid BST gives a strictly increasing list. Check that list.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Range bounds passed down (no list).
steps: valid(node, low, high): null → true.
If node.val <= low or node.val >= high → false.
Return valid(left, low, node.val) && valid(right, node.val, high).
Use long bounds (Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE) because node values can be Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE.
approaches.why: Each node is checked once against its interval, and we stop at the first violation; only the recursion stack is used.
approaches.simple: Pass down an allowed range (low, high). Each node must sit inside its range, and it narrows the range for its children.

title: Kth Smallest / Largest Element in a BST
problem: Given the root of a BST and an integer k (1-indexed), return the k-th smallest value in the tree. Striver also asks for the k-th largest.
example: Explanation: Sorted values are [1,2,3,4]; the 1st smallest is 1 and the 1st largest is 4.
intuition: Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order. So the k-th smallest is simply the k-th node visited by inorder. The k-th largest is the k-th node visited by reverse inorder (right, node, left).

The brute force ignores the BST structure (collect + sort). The better one uses inorder but walks the whole tree. The optimal one stops the moment it has visited k nodes, which matters when k is small and the tree is huge.
notes: Say it like this: "Collect-and-sort is O(n log n). Since BST inorder is sorted, the k-th inorder node is the answer, O(n) with a list. Doing inorder iteratively and stopping at the k-th pop is O(h + k) time and O(h) space. For k-th largest I do reverse inorder: right, node, left."
Edge cases: k = 1 (minimum) and k = n (maximum); skewed BST; duplicates if allowed (still works, they appear consecutively).
Common mistakes: JS sort() without a comparator (sorts as strings); off-by-one with 1-indexed k; k-th largest computed as vals[k].

Follow-ups: "The BST is modified often and kthSmallest is called often?" — augment each node with the size of its left subtree; then walk down in O(h): if k <= leftSize go left, if k == leftSize + 1 return node, else go right with k -= leftSize + 1. Construct Binary Tree From 6.13
simple: Find the k-th smallest (or largest) value in a BST.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Collect all values with any traversal.
Sort them.
Return vals[k-1] (smallest) or vals[n-k] (largest).
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; we store every value.
approaches.simple: Collect all values, sort, pick the k-th.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: Full recursive inorder into a list (already sorted, no sort needed), then index.
approaches.why: One full traversal; the list holds all n values.
approaches.simple: In-order traversal already gives sorted values; pick the k-th.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Iterative inorder with a stack, stopping at the k-th pop. For k-th largest, mirror it (go right first).
steps: Push all left nodes from the current node onto the stack.
Pop: that's the next smallest. Decrement k; if k hits 0, return its value.
Move to the popped node's right child and repeat.
approaches.why: We first descend h nodes to the minimum, then pop k nodes (each pop may push a few more, amortized O(1)); the stack never holds more than one root-to-leaf path.
approaches.simple: Do the in-order walk with a stack and stop as soon as you have counted k nodes.

title: Construct Binary Tree From Preorder And Inorder Traversal
problem: Given the preorder and inorder traversal arrays of a binary tree with unique values, rebuild and return the tree.
example: Explanation: 3 is the root (first in preorder). In inorder, [9] is left of 3 and [15,20,7] is right of 3;
intuition: Two facts: 1. The first element of preorder is the root. 2. In inorder, everything left of the root belongs to the left subtree and everything right belongs to the right subtree. So the root's position in inorder tells you the left subtree's size, leftSize.
Then in preorder, after the root, the next leftSize elements are the left subtree's preorder and the rest are the right subtree's. Recurse on both halves.
Trace: pre [3,9,20,15,7], in [9,3,15,20,7]. Root 3 at inorder index 1 → leftSize 1. Left: pre [9], in [9]. Right: pre [20,15,7], in [15,20,7] → root 20, left 15, right 7.

The brute force searches for the root in inorder linearly every time (and copies sub-arrays). The optimal precomputes value → inorder index in a hash map and uses index ranges instead of copies; it also consumes preorder with a single moving pointer, because preorder order (root, left, right) is exactly the order we create nodes in.
notes: Say it like this: "Preorder's first element is the root; its position in inorder splits the left and right subtrees. Searching linearly and slicing arrays is O(n²). With a value-to-index map and inorder index ranges, plus a single pointer walking preorder, each node is built in O(1): O(n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: single node; fully left-skewed or right-skewed trees (deep recursion); empty arrays.

Common mistakes: building the right subtree before the left when using the shared preIdx pointer; off-by-one in ranges; assuming it works with duplicate values (it doesn't — the problem guarantees uniqueness).

Follow-ups: "Inorder + postorder?" (LC 106) — root is the LAST element of postorder; consume postorder from the end and build the right subtree first. "Preorder + postorder?" — not unique in general (LC 889 returns any valid tree). 6.14
simple: Rebuild a tree from its preorder and inorder lists.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: If preorder is empty, return null.
Root = preorder[0]; find its index mid in inorder by linear scan.
Left = build(preorder[1..mid], inorder[0..mid-1]); Right = build(preorder[mid+1..], inorder[mid+1..]), using array copies.
approaches.why: Each call does an O(n) search and O(n) copying; with a skewed tree there are n levels of recursion, so both work and total copied memory are quadratic.
approaches.simple: The first preorder value is the root; find it in inorder by scanning to split left and right parts, and recurse.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Build a hash map value → index in inorder.
Keep a global pointer preIdx into preorder, starting at 0.
build(lo, hi) builds the subtree whose inorder range is [lo, hi]: if lo > hi return null; root = preorder[preIdx++]; mid = map[root]; build left with [lo, mid-1] first, then right with [mid+1, hi].
approaches.why: Each node is created once with an O(1) map lookup; the map is O(n) and the recursion stack is O(h) ≤ O(n).
approaches.simple: Same idea, but a map gives the root's position in inorder instantly.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
pattern: Tree DFS (return one branch, update global with both)
problem: A path is any sequence of nodes connected by edges where each node appears at most once; it does not need to pass through the root and must contain at least one node. Return the maximum sum of node values over all paths. Values can be negative.
example: Explanation: The best path is 15 -> 20 -> 7 with sum 15 + 20 + 7 = 42.
intuition: This is the diameter problem with values instead of edge counts. Every path has a highest node where it turns. At that node, the best path is node.val + bestDown(left) + bestDown(right), where bestDown(x) is the best sum of a path that starts at x and goes downward along one branch.

Two twists compared to diameter: 1. A downward branch with a negative sum only hurts, so we can choose not to take it: use max(0, bestDown(child)). 2. What we return to the parent is a single branch, node.val + max(leftGain, rightGain), because a path coming up from the parent can't fork into both children. What we record globally is the forked version with both gains.
Trace on [-10,9,20,null,null,15,7]: gain(15)=15, gain(7)=7. At 20: path 20+15+7 = 42 → best=42; return 20+15=35. gain(9)=9 (best stays 42). At −10: path −10+9+35 = 34 < 42. Answer 42.
notes: Say it like this: "Every path peaks at some node, where its sum is node + best left branch + best right branch, ignoring negative branches. Recomputing branch gains per node is O(n²). In one post-order DFS I return the best single branch upward and update a global max with the forked path at each node: O(n) time, O(h) space."
Edge cases: all negative values (answer is the max single node, e.g. [-3] → −3); single node; best path entirely inside one subtree, not touching the root.

Common mistakes: initializing best = 0; returning node.val + leftGain + rightGain to the parent (that's a fork, not a path); forgetting max(0,...); overflow is not an issue here with LeetCode limits (≤ 3·10⁴ nodes, |val| ≤ 1000), but mention long for larger values.

Follow-ups: "Return the path itself?" — store which child gave each gain and reconstruct from the best node. "Max path between two leaves?" (GfG) — only update the global when both children exist. 6.15
simple: Find the path with the biggest sum of values (any start, any end).

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Write gain(node) = node.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)) (best downward path starting at node), computed from scratch.
For every node, compute node.val + max(0, gain(left)) + max(0, gain(right)).
Return the maximum over all nodes.
approaches.why: gain re-walks the whole subtree for every node; on a skewed tree that's n + (n−1) +... = O(n²).
approaches.simple: For every node, compute the best downward paths on each side from scratch.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: One post-order DFS.
steps: dfs(null) = 0.
leftGain = max(0, dfs(left)), rightGain = max(0, dfs(right)).
best = max(best, node.val + leftGain + rightGain) — path turning here.
Return node.val + max(leftGain, rightGain) — one branch for the parent.
Initialize best to Integer.MIN_VALUE (not 0), so an all-negative tree returns its largest single value.
approaches.why: O(1) work per node in a single pass; only the recursion stack.
approaches.simple: Each node returns its best downward gain (ignoring negative sides) and updates the best path that bends at it.

title: Serialize And Deserialize Binary Tree
pattern: Preorder DFS with null markers / BFS
problem: Design a Codec with serialize(root) that converts a binary tree into a string and deserialize(data) that rebuilds exactly the same tree from that string. Any format is allowed as long as the round trip is exact.
example: Explanation: deserialize(serialize(root)) must give back a tree identical to root, e.g. via the string
intuition: A single traversal like preorder [1,2,3,4,5] isn't enough to rebuild a tree — many shapes share it. (That's why 6.13 needed two traversals.) The fix is to also write down the null children. Once nulls are recorded, a preorder sequence pins down the tree uniquely: reading it back, every token is either "null, stop here" or "a node, now build its left subtree, then its right subtree" — the same recursion used to write it.
Both BFS (the LeetCode display format) and preorder DFS work in O(n). Preorder DFS is shorter to write and mirrors serialize/deserialize perfectly, which is why it's the usual interview answer.
notes: Say it like this: "A traversal alone is ambiguous, but if I also write null children, preorder uniquely defines the tree. Serialize is a preorder DFS writing '#' for nulls; deserialize reads tokens in the same order with a pointer and rebuilds recursively. Both are O(n) time and space. BFS with null markers also works and avoids deep recursion on skewed trees."
Edge cases: empty tree; negative and multi-digit values (need a delimiter); skewed tree of 10⁴ nodes (recursion depth — mention the BFS version or an explicit stack).

Common mistakes: no delimiter between values; no null markers; using a static field for the pointer (breaks with concurrent/multiple Codec uses); string concatenation with += in a loop in Java (O(n²)) instead of StringBuilder.

Follow-ups: "Serialize a BST more compactly?" (LC 449) — preorder without null markers is enough, since bounds tell you where each subtree ends. "N-ary tree?" — write each node's child count after its value. 6.16
simple: Turn a tree into a string and back again.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: BFS level order with null markers (LeetCode's own format).
steps: Serialize: BFS from the root; append each node's value, or # for null; for non-null nodes, enqueue both children (even null ones).
Deserialize: the first token is the root; keep a queue of nodes waiting for children, and assign the next two tokens as the left and right child of each polled node.
approaches.why: Each node and each null child is written and read once (there are n + 1 nulls); the string and the queue are O(n).
approaches.simple: Write values level by level with # for empty spots; read them back level by level.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Preorder DFS with null markers.
steps: Serialize: write(node): null → append #; else append value, then write(left), write(right).
Deserialize: split into tokens, keep a pointer; read(): take the next token; # → return null; else create the node, set left = read(), right = read().
approaches.why: Each node and null marker is written and parsed exactly once; the string/token array is O(n), recursion stack O(h).
approaches.simple: Write values in preorder with # for empty spots; read them back recursively in the same order.

title: Maximum Width of BT
problem: The width of a level is the number of positions between its leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes, counting the null gaps in between as if the tree were complete. Return the maximum width over all levels (LeetCode 662: Maximum Width of Binary Tree). The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
example: Explanation: The last level is 5, 3, null, 9: from the 5 to the 9 there are 4 positions (including the null
intuition: Number the nodes like a heap: root is index 0, left child of i is 2i + 1, right child is 2i + 2. Then the width of a level is simply lastIndex − firstIndex + 1, and null gaps are automatically counted because the missing nodes still "own" their indices.

The catch: indices double every level, so on a deep skewed tree they overflow even long (depth 3000 means 2³⁰⁰⁰). Fix: at the start of every level, subtract the level's first index from every index in that level. Widths are differences, so shifting doesn't change them, and the numbers stay small (bounded by about 2 × width). The brute force literally builds each level including null placeholders — easy to understand, but the number of placeholders explodes exponentially on deep sparse trees.
notes: Say it like this: "Width counts null gaps, so I give each node its heap index — children 2i+1 and 2i+2 — and width is last minus first plus one per level. Materializing nulls is exponential on deep sparse trees. BFS with indices is O(n) time and O(width) space, and I subtract the level's first index each time so the indices don't overflow."
Edge cases: single node → 1; a skewed chain (width 1 at every level, but raw indices would reach 2^depth); levels where only the far-left and far-right nodes exist.
Common mistakes: counting only non-null nodes per level; not normalizing indices (overflow in Java, precision loss in JS beyond 2⁵³); computing width as size of the queue.

Follow-ups: "DFS version?" — pass (depth, index), store the first index seen at each depth in a list, and compute index − first[depth] + 1 at every node; O(n) time, O(h) space. "Vertical order traversal?" (LC 987) — a related indexing idea using column = −1/+1 instead of heap indices.
simple: Find the widest level, counting the gaps between the end nodes.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: BFS where each level is a list that may contain nulls; for every slot (null or not), push two children (nulls for a null slot).
Trim leading and trailing nulls from the new level; if it's empty, stop.
Width of a level = its length after trimming; track the max.
approaches.why: Null placeholders double each level, so a deep sparse tree (e.g., a zigzag chain) can make levels exponentially long. Fine for tiny trees only; it's here to show why indexing is needed.
approaches.simple: Go level by level, including empty spots as placeholders. It explodes for deep trees.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: BFS storing (node, index), with indices normalized per level.
steps: Queue holds pairs (node, idx); start with (root, 0).
For each level: first = index of the first node in the queue; size = queue.size().
Pop each node; let i = idx − first (normalized). Track last = i. Push children with 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
Width of the level = last + 1 (since the first normalized index is 0); track the max.
approaches.why: Each real node is processed once (nulls are never enqueued); the queue holds one level. Indices are long in Java as a safety margin, though normalization already keeps them small.
approaches.simple: Number nodes like a heap (children 2i+1 and 2i+2). Width of a level = last number − first number + 1.
